summary: The main difference between a cheetah and a leopard is build and lifestyle: the cheetah is a slim, long-legged daytime sprinter with solid black spots, while the leopard is a stockier, more powerful night hunter with rosette markings. Cheetahs have black tear lines running from the eyes to the mouth. Leopards lack them and are expert climbers that haul prey into trees.

differences.title: Spots
differences.text: A cheetah's coat is covered in simple, solid black spots, evenly spaced like dots from a marker. A leopard has rosettes, which are clusters of dark spots arranged in a broken ring around a slightly darker center. Leopard spots become solid only on the head, legs and belly. This is the most reliable difference in photographs.

differences.title: Face markings
differences.text: Every cheetah has a black tear mark on each side of the face, running from the inner corner of the eye down to the mouth. These lines may help cut glare during daytime hunts. Leopards have no tear marks. Their faces are broader and heavier, with small spots and a more powerful jaw.

differences.title: Body build
differences.text: The cheetah is built like a greyhound, with a small head, deep chest, narrow waist, long legs and a flexible spine that lengthens each stride. The leopard is lower, longer and far more muscular, with a big skull and thick neck. Leopards are generally the heavier cat, even though cheetahs stand taller at the shoulder.

differences.title: Claws
differences.text: Cheetah claws are only semi-retractable. They stay partly exposed and work like the spikes on running shoes, giving grip in high-speed turns, but they are blunt. A leopard's claws retract fully into sheaths and stay razor sharp, which lets it grip struggling prey and climb tree trunks with ease.

differences.title: Hunting and activity
differences.text: Cheetahs hunt mostly by day, stalking within range and then running down gazelles and other small antelope in a short, extremely fast chase. Leopards hunt mainly at night by ambush, creeping close and pouncing. A leopard often drags its kill up a tree, out of reach of lions and hyenas. Cheetahs frequently lose kills to other predators.

differences.title: Voice and classification
differences.text: The leopard is a true big cat in the genus Panthera and can roar, producing a rasping call that sounds like sawing wood. The cheetah is the only living member of the genus Acinonyx and cannot roar. Instead it purrs, chirps like a bird and makes a stuttering call.

similarities: Cheetahs and leopards are both spotted members of the cat family, Felidae, and share a golden coat that blends into dry grass and dappled shade. Both are solitary for much of their lives, both prey mainly on small and medium-sized antelope, and their ranges overlap across much of Africa. Both species are classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.
howToTell: Look for black tear lines from the eyes to the mouth. Only the cheetah has them.
Check the spot pattern: solid round dots mean cheetah; ring-shaped rosettes mean leopard.
A spotted cat lying on a tree branch, especially with a carcass, is a leopard.
A lean, long-legged spotted cat scanning open plains in daylight, often from a termite mound, is likely a cheetah.

faq.question: Who would win a fight, a cheetah or a leopard?
faq.answer: A leopard would almost certainly win. It is heavier, far more muscular and armed with sharp retractable claws and a stronger bite. Cheetahs are built for speed, not combat, and avoid confrontation because any injury could stop them from hunting. In the wild, leopards occasionally kill cheetahs.

faq.question: Which is faster, a cheetah or a leopard?
faq.answer: The cheetah is much faster. It is the fastest land animal, capable of explosive acceleration over short distances, while the leopard relies on stealth and only needs a brief rush to reach its prey. The comparison table above lists the top speeds recorded for each species.

faq.question: Can cheetahs and leopards interbreed?
faq.answer: No. Cheetahs and leopards belong to different genera, Acinonyx and Panthera, and are only distantly related within the cat family. The cheetah's closest living relatives are actually the cougar and the jaguarundi. No cheetah–leopard hybrid has ever been documented.

faq.question: Is a cheetah or a leopard more dangerous to humans?
faq.answer: The leopard is far more dangerous. Leopards are powerful, live close to people in parts of Africa and Asia, and occasionally attack humans. Wild cheetahs are timid, and there are no verified records of a wild cheetah killing a person.
